opportunities.title: France family skipass pricing — stop buying Alps tickets like they're Breckenridge
opportunities.whyItMatters: Two kids on US-style window logic for a week in the Alps is how a fun trip turns into a financial own-goal. French resorts still price children and family packs like they actually want families to show up.
opportunities.howItWorks: Most major French ski areas sell a family skipass (typically 2 adults + 2 children) and a steep youth rate that has nothing in common with a $200 Colorado walk-up. You buy the pack from the resort or its official skipass site — not a US reseller — for the specific dates of your trip.
opportunities.whyYouQualify: Two adults, two kids (8 and 12), and a France destination already on your list. Youth pricing covers both children at the resorts in play. No Vermont residency required. This one is about who is in the family, not where you live.
opportunities.recommendedAction: Before you book lodging, pick the resort and buy the official family/youth skipass for your dates. Do not price this trip using US adult ticket numbers.
opportunities.deadline: Buy once dates are firm — family packs are usually date-specific and not something you want to do at the window in a jet-lagged fog.
restrictions: Kids must be within the resort's published youth age band (your 8- and 12-year-old both clear the usual 5–17 window, but confirm the exact ages at your resort).
Family packs usually require the same dates and the same domain.
Insurance, photos, and hands-free cards can add a little. I did not count those as savings or as gotchas worth panic.

opportunities.title: Breckenridge is not on Ikon. Don't pay window prices to find that out.
opportunities.whyItMatters: Sugarbush being an Ikon mountain does nothing for you in Summit County. If this trip happens on window tickets, you will light real money on fire in the name of convenience.
opportunities.howItWorks: Epic Day Pass (or the smallest Epic product that covers your Breck days) is the grown-up version of this trip. You buy it in advance from Epic, then skip the window. The earlier you buy, the less it costs. This is not a secret. It is also not what most families do when they already 'have a pass.'
opportunities.whyYouQualify: Breckenridge is on your destination list, you ski enough days to make a short Epic product cheaper than three or four full-price tickets, and Ikon does not cover this mountain.
opportunities.recommendedAction: Count the Breck days. Buy the matching Epic Day Pass now, not in Colorado. If the trip is still a maybe, wait — this save only counts if you actually go.
opportunities.deadline: Epic Day Pass pricing steps up in tiers through fall. The cheap version is the early one.
restrictions: Blackout dates and mountain restrictions depend on the exact Epic product. Read the calendar before you buy.
This does not stack with Ikon. I did not pretend it does.
If the Breck trip gets dropped, this opportunity disappears with it.

opportunities.title: Bolton Valley stops being a window-ticket mountain at your day count
opportunities.whyItMatters: Bolton is close, friendly, and dangerously easy to overpay for one day at a time. At 16–30 family days, some of those days are going to land here. Window math assumes they won't.
opportunities.howItWorks: Bolton's season pass and multi-day products undercut repeated window tickets once you stop treating the mountain like a backup plan. You do not need everyone on a pass. You need the people who will actually ski it on one.
opportunities.whyYouQualify: Bolton is a listed home mountain, you live in 05404 (that's not a long drive), and your season volume is in the range where a pass or pack beats improvising.
opportunities.recommendedAction: Decide who actually skis Bolton. Put those people on a Bolton product. Leave the others off. Do not buy four of everything.
opportunities.deadline: Preseason pass pricing is the whole point. After that you're just buying a slightly cheaper window ticket.
restrictions: Only counts if you will actually ski Bolton more than a couple of times.
Do not double-count this against a day that was already going on Ikon at Sugarbush.

opportunities.title: Smuggs family products — you listed it, so stop paying like tourists
opportunities.whyItMatters: Smuggs is built for families and then quietly prices day tickets like it isn't. If it's on your mountain list, there is almost always a better product than four walk-up tickets and a shrug.
opportunities.howItWorks: Look at their family packages, stay-and-ski deals, and youth pricing before you Google 'Smuggs tickets' the night before. The family-shaped products are the ones that move the number.
opportunities.whyYouQualify: Two school-age kids, Smugglers' Notch on the destination list, and a season that already includes mixed Vermont days.
opportunities.recommendedAction: If Smuggs is more than a one-off, buy the family-shaped product. If it's a one-off, this is not a jackpot — skip it without guilt.
opportunities.deadline: Package rates are better when lodging and lift are booked together, not as two separate panic purchases.
restrictions: Lodging packages only help if you were going to stay over anyway.
I did not count kids-camp upsells as 'savings.'

opportunities.title: Youth pricing for the 12-year-old is not the same as 'the kid pass you already know'
opportunities.whyItMatters: A 7th grader is in the awkward zone: too old for the cute free programs, young enough that youth products still matter. Families often leave them on the adult-ish option out of inertia.
opportunities.howItWorks: Confirm the Ikon/Sugarbush youth product for a 12-year-old and whether the 8-year-old is on the correct child product. Wrong product here doesn't look dramatic. It just leaks money all season.
opportunities.whyYouQualify: You have a 12-year-old and a 8-year-old, Sugarbush is a home mountain, and Ikon is already part of the picture.
opportunities.recommendedAction: Pull up the exact product each person holds. If the 12-year-old is on anything adult-flavored, fix it before the season starts.
restrictions: Depends on the exact Ikon product in the house — that's one of the unknowns.
Not counted as a jackpot because it might already be correct.

opportunities.title: Lesson packages beat buying one private lesson as an apology
opportunities.whyItMatters: If a kid is getting a lesson this year, buying it as a one-off is the most expensive way to do a nice thing.
opportunities.howItWorks: Most of your mountains sell multi-lesson packs or first-timer bundles that undercut the single-lesson rate. Only useful if lessons are actually happening.
opportunities.whyYouQualify: School-age kids and a mix of mountains that all sell lesson products. No lesson plans? Ignore this one.
opportunities.recommendedAction: If anyone is taking a lesson, buy a pack at the mountain they'll actually use. Don't collect lesson vouchers like frequent-flyer miles.

opportunities.title: Rentals: one seasonal setup vs. four window pickups
opportunities.whyItMatters: Window rentals are priced for people who forgot their skis. Seasonal rentals are priced for people who live here. You live here.
opportunities.howItWorks: A seasonal rental for the kid who's still growing usually beats repeating demo-shop visits, especially if Bolton/Smuggs/Sugarbush days add up.
opportunities.whyYouQualify: Local-ish family, two kids, 16–30 days. If everybody owns gear that fits, this one is already handled.
opportunities.recommendedAction: If the 8-year-old is still in rental gear, go seasonal. If not, skip it. I'm not going to invent a save.

steps.title: Price the France trip on a family skipass, not on US adult tickets
steps.description: This is the biggest number on the page. Pick the resort, then buy the official family/youth pack for your dates before lodging gets so locked that you stop caring about lift math.

steps.title: Buy an Epic Day Pass for Breckenridge — or drop the trip from the savings story
steps.description: Ikon will not help you in Summit County. If you're going, buy Epic early. If you're not going, this $400–$650 disappears, and that's fine.

steps.title: Stop window-ticketing Bolton
steps.description: Decide who actually skis it and put them on a Bolton product while preseason pricing still exists.

steps.title: Confirm the Ikon product on every body in the house
steps.description: Especially the 12-year-old. Wrong product here is quiet and expensive.

knownSavings.title: Ikon access for Sugarbush
knownSavings.note: You already told me this is in the mix, so I verified it and then left it out of the discovery total. I'm not going to high-five myself for a pass you already bought.

watch.title: Vermont 5th Grade Ski Passport
watch.whatWeAreWatching: The statewide 5th-grade passport that unlocks a pile of Vermont mountains for a ridiculous price.
watch.whyItCouldMatter: Your 8-year-old is in 3rd grade. This isn't a save this season. It is absolutely a save the year they hit 5th.
watch.expectedTiming: Two seasons out — watch for the 2028–29 registration window.
watch.trigger: Kid enters 5th grade and Ski Vermont opens registration.

watch.title: Ikon spring renewal / price step-ups
watch.whatWeAreWatching: Ikon's spring and early-summer price locks, plus any family or youth product changes.
watch.whyItCouldMatter: If Ikon stays your Sugarbush answer, buying it in the first window is the difference between a smart pass and an expensive habit.
watch.expectedTiming: Spring 2027, usually with a deadline that arrives earlier than people remember.
watch.trigger: Ikon publishes 2027–28 pricing or your current product changes.

methodology.title: No fake wins
methodology.text: I don't count programs you already knew about as discoveries, I don't double-count overlapping savings, and I leave uncertain upside out of the headline number.

referralLine: Know another ski family getting murdered by lift-ticket prices? Send them to SkiFamilySavings.com.
